one_liner: Small (2600-line) thread-caching general-purpose allocator for 64-bit Windows/Linux that beats the MSVC CRT malloc on its own alloc/free stress tests.
what_it_does: A general-purpose malloc replacement with a KanameShiki::Alloc/Free/Align/ReAlloc/Size API, plus global operator new/delete overrides (New.cpp) and, on Linux, malloc/free/calloc/realloc/posix_memalign symbols for LD_PRELOAD (Posix.cpp). It is built as one translation unit (src/KanameShiki.cpp includes the other .cpp files) into a static .lib on MSVC or a shared .so on g++/clang++. Two compile-time profiles: cooperative (KANAMESHIKI_HEAP_SPECIALIZATION=0, 8 MiB global heap) and specialized (=1, 8 GiB global heap reserved and committed up front, aimed at consoles/embedded).
how_it_is_fast: Size-segregated per-thread allocators: LocalPool (fixed-size pools in 8-byte classes up to 1 KiB), LocalCram (power-of-two classes up to 1 MiB) and LocalAny (one OS mapping per block above 1 MiB). Each has an own-thread free list touched with no atomics and a remote-free list split across several slots; the 'RevolverAtomic' scheme rotates an atomic index on every remote free so concurrent CAS pushes spread over different cache lines instead of contending on one head (Cache.h). Freed pools and blocks are kept in local and global reserver free lists before falling back to a mutex-protected first-fit global heap (doubly linked nodes with coalescing) and then VirtualAlloc/mmap, so repeated large alloc/free pairs avoid OS calls.
when_to_use: Windows x64 programs (MSVC) whose hot path is malloc/free or new/delete churn of small blocks up to 1 KiB across 8 or so threads, where the CRT heap is the bottleneck.
Producer/consumer patterns where blocks are allocated on one thread and freed on another (the benchmark's testF-testI), which the per-slot remote free lists target.
Console or embedded-style programs that own the machine and can afford the specialized profile's 8 GiB up-front reservation in exchange for fewer OS calls.
As a small, readable reference design for thread-caching allocators (about 49 KB of source, MIT).
when_not_to_use: When mimalloc is an option: in the author's own single-thread runs mimalloc is faster (0B-1KiB alloc-only 0.022 s vs 0.036 s; with memory fill 0.209 s vs 0.223 s), and with memory fill in the 2MiB-32MiB 8-thread test mimalloc total is 3085.8 s vs 3730.7 s.
Long-running services that need memory returned to the OS: the large-block speedups come from caching freed blocks in reserver lists, and the specialized profile commits 8 GiB at start-up.

Production code that needs a maintained allocator: no commits since 2019-10-19, an open unanswered segfault report in the cooperative profile (issue #3, crash in GlobalReserver::Alloc), and the README says MinGW64 g++ and clang++ builds do not work.
Programs that use posix_memalign/memalign/valloc through the LD_PRELOAD shim (see gotchas), or 32-bit and pre-Haswell x86 targets (the code uses _lzcnt/_tzcnt and assumes 8-byte size_t).

integration.form: static lib (MSVC) or shared lib (g++/clang++ LD_PRELOAD); single-TU source-drop also possible
integration.dependencies: none beyond the C++ standard library and the OS (VirtualAlloc or mmap); -lpthread -latomic on Linux
integration.min_toolchain: C++14 (clang++ -std=c++14 in README); MSVC version not stated; g++ build needs -mlzcnt -mbmi
integration.platforms: x86-64 only in practice (LZCNT/BMI1 intrinsics, 64-bit size_t constants); Windows 10 and Linux; MinGW64 not working
integration.thread_safety: Thread-safe; own-thread lists are lock-free and wait-free, remote-free and global reserver lists use CAS, the global heap uses a std::mutex; per-thread state lives in thread_local LocalCntx.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — on Linux LD_PRELOAD replaces malloc/free/calloc/realloc; on Windows only operator new/delete are replaced and C code must call KanameShiki::Alloc/Free explicitly (the benchmark does exactly that)

gotchas: memalign(alignment, size) in src/Posix.cpp calls aligned_alloc(size, alignment) with the arguments swapped, so posix_memalign/memalign/valloc return ENOMEM/nullptr for most size/alignment pairs and an under-aligned block when alignment exceeds size. The published benchmark does not exercise this path.
calloc computes nmemb * size with no overflow check, so an overflowing request returns a block smaller than asked for; realloc always allocates a new block and copies, even when shrinking.

The benchmark's alloc-then-immediately-free loops (testA) reward block caching: mimalloc times about 0.001 s and KanameShiki is similar, while the CRT pays OS-level costs for 2MiB-32MiB blocks (single-thread total 17.05 s vs 0.006 s). In FILL mode Main.cpp re-enables assert and checks every byte in a loop before freeing, so those totals are dominated by the harness's own memset and verify passes.

Builds differ: the mimalloc binary is linked with -MD -LTCG while malloc, tcmalloc, jemalloc and KanameShiki use the default static CRT; jemalloc 'segfaults frequently' on the author's MSVC build and mimalloc had 234,674 failed allocations in c4 testI (8 threads x 128 blocks of up to 32 MiB exceeds the 32 GiB machine).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over fc_malloc or the hobby allocators (Bloodmoon001, atul-singh-as) when you need cross-thread frees and a full malloc surface on Windows with numbers against mimalloc/jemalloc/tcmalloc; pick a maintained allocator such as mimalloc or IsoAlloc instead for production, and Mesh when memory footprint matters more than speed.
verified_claims_summary: On a Core i7-8700 under Windows 10 with MSVC cl -Ox, the author's harness (Main.cpp, nine tests, 8 threads) totals 1.73 s for 0B-1KiB vs 2.33 s for the MSVC CRT malloc (about 1.35x, derived from page data) and 1.90 s for mimalloc, and 3.22 s vs 89.80 s for 2MiB-32MiB alloc+free only; with memory fill the large-block gap shrinks to 3730.7 s vs 6186.0 s and mimalloc is faster. Raw timings are in Benchmark/*.txt; the MSVC version is not stated and nobody else has reproduced them.
status_note: Abandoned since 2019-10-19 with open crash and benchmark-source issues; MIT and small enough to vendor or study, but treat it as a reference design rather than a production allocator.
